passage: I'm Sabina. In Class 6 I made a joke about Bhupen's old school bag, and half the class hooted. It felt like being lit up from inside. So I made another joke the next day, and another. But the cheering was thin. The moment I stopped, the same faces turned to their notebooks, and nobody asked me to sit with them at lunch. Bhupen never looked up at me at all; he ate alone by the window. That afternoon I understood that those claps had never meant respect. I stopped the jokes, and at lunch I offered him half my orange. He looked surprised and said thanks, very quietly.

qa.q: What did Sabina make a joke about?
qa.a: Sabina made a joke about Bhupen's old school bag.

qa.q: Why did Sabina stop making jokes about Bhupen?
qa.a: Sabina saw that the cheering was thin and faded once the jokes stopped, and understood it had never meant real respect.

qa.q: What did Sabina do after stopping the jokes, and why might it matter to Bhupen?
qa.a: Sabina offered him half an orange at lunch, a small kind step that showed him respect after the mockery.

qa.q: How might Bhupen have felt eating alone by the window while the class cheered the jokes?
qa.a: He was probably hurt and lonely, since he never looked up at Sabina and ate by himself.

grounding: A child mocks a classmate for the applause, sees the cheering is empty, and chooses respect.

passage:
At their school in Osaka, Hana had found a way to make the whole class laugh: copying the careful, slow way Jin read aloud. Every time she did it, the back row cheered, and Hana felt powerful, like the star of a show.
By the third week, though, something changed. When teams were picked for the science project, nobody picked Hana. At lunch, the same kids who had cheered talked about her in low voices. One girl said, "She's funny, but I wouldn't trust her."
Hana stared at her rice. The cheering had felt so big. Now it felt like nothing.
The next time Jin read aloud, Hana kept quiet. Afterwards she said, "Your reading was good today, Jin."

qa.q: What did Hana copy to make the class laugh?
qa.a: The careful, slow way Jin read aloud.

qa.q: What was Hana feeling when nobody picked her for the science project?
qa.a: She felt hurt and empty, realising the cheering had not turned into real respect.

qa.q: What did Hana choose instead of more mocking, and why was it wiser?
qa.a: She stayed quiet and complimented Jin, choosing respect over thin applause that had already faded.

qa.q: How might the girl who said she wouldn't trust Hana see her?
qa.a: The girl sees Hana as entertaining but unkind, someone who might turn the jokes on anyone.

grounding: A girl feels powerful when classmates cheer her mockery, but the applause fades and they do not respect her, so she stops and chooses respect.

passage:
At the dance academy, Alka liked to copy Ishita's wobbly turns during water breaks. The other girls clapped and squealed. Alka took a bow each time.
But on the evening of the class show, Alka forgot her steps on stage. Afterwards, in the changing room, she waited for the girls to comfort her. Nobody came. They were all around Ishita, helping her with her hairpins.
Alka heard one of them whisper, "Now she knows how it feels."
Her face burned. The clapping had never really been for her.
The next practice, when Ishita wobbled, Alka didn't copy her. She said, "Try leaning a bit forward. It helped me."

qa.q: Where did Alka copy Ishita's turns?
qa.a: At the dance academy, during water breaks.

qa.q: How did Alka feel when nobody came to comfort her?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and alone, realising the girls who clapped had not really been on her side.

qa.q: What did Alka do differently at the next practice?
qa.a: Instead of mocking Ishita, she offered a helpful tip, choosing respect over applause.

qa.q: How might Ishita feel when Alka gives her the tip?
qa.a: Ishita may feel surprised and a little wary, but also relieved to be helped instead of mocked.

grounding: A girl enjoys her classmates clapping when she mocks another dancer, then sees they do not respect her, and chooses to help instead.
